G1:
The obvious objection to our plan is that Laura holds too few shares. She has years to go, a building to fund, and shares grow – so surely more of the 2028 deposit belongs in VT? But for Laura, more shares is the risky choice: it buys a little more on average and costs her what she most needs in 2031, a figure she can promise.

The money in question is about $111,700, left from the 2028 deposit after the top-up. Our plan puts about 55% of the $150,000 into the Treasury fund maturing in late 2032 and the rest into VT. Half of VT moves into Treasuries before the 2031 meetings, the range is only what she then owns in Treasuries, and the other half is her flexibility. The plan is frozen; we simply ran it against the alternatives in 200,000 simulated futures (6 November curve).

Ours states $95,000 to $115,000 and contributes $115,000 at the median, $95,000 in a bad 1-in-20 future, and under $95,000 in about 3 in 100. Put three-quarters of the $111,700 in shares. Everything Laura has beyond the 10 payments rises by about $7,000 at the median, and her flexibility more than doubles, from about $29,000 to $66,000 – that's the appeal. The catch is everything else. A bad 1-in-20 future leaves her about $14,000 worse off, the range she can state drops to $30,000–$85,000, and the contribution misses $95,000 in about 62 futures in 100. All shares is worse again: no floor, $0 to $70,000, and a miss in 79 in 100.

To be fair, all-floor isn't free either: it states a single $130,000 in about 95 futures in 100, but leaves her less in total than our plan in about 63, with only about $9,000 of flexibility.

In other words, shares add to what she keeps; only Treasuries add to what she can promise. The case warns that overpromising would damage her credibility – and we'd rather hand her a number she'll never have to walk back than an extra $7,000 at the median.
G2:
The usual instinct, saving for a building 5 years away, is shares, and plenty of them – Laura has time, and shares grow. Our plan does close to the opposite with the 2028 deposit, because for Laura, more shares is the risky choice.

The reason is that ink only goes one way. As one illustrator put it, adding ink is easy, whereas taking it away "is a lot more complicated (and messy)" (Richmond, 2006). Laura's promise in 2031 behaves exactly like that. She can always give co-sponsors more than she named; giving less is the messy kind, and the case says overpromising would damage her credibility. So the plan inks only what she owns. Both ends of the range are rounded down, anything above the top goes to her flexibility, and half of VT stays in pencil on purpose. More shares simply means more pencil – and less she can ink.

The model agrees (200,000 simulated futures, 6 November curve; benchmarks only, as the plan is frozen). About $111,700 is split after the top-up: about 55% of the $150,000 deposit into the late-2032 Treasury fund, the rest into VT, half of which is inked before the 2031 meetings. That states $95,000 to $115,000 and contributes $115,000 at the median, $95,000 in a bad 1-in-20 future and under $95,000 in about 3 in 100, with about $29,000 of flexibility.

With three-quarters in shares, her median total beyond the 10 payments gains about $7,000 and her flexibility reaches about $66,000. In exchange, her bad 1-in-20 total loses about $14,000, the range she can ink shrinks to $30,000–$85,000, and 62 in 100 come in under $95,000. All shares leaves nothing to ink at the bottom: $0 to $70,000, and 79 in 100 short.

Inking everything has its own price – a single $130,000 in about 95 futures in 100, but less in total than our plan in about 63, and only about $9,000 of flexibility. So the plan leaves enough in pencil for the shares to grow, and inks nothing it might need to take back.
G3:
The first plan we built for Laura would have been a mistake, and our own model told us so before we'd placed a single trade.

On Sunday 27 September that plan put about three-quarters of the money in shares and trusted 10 years of growth to cover the 10 payments. We genuinely believed 10 years was long enough for shares to carry them. Then we tested it. In our simulations that day, it missed at least one payment in 3.2% of markets – in 13.7% if the 2028 deposit came in at $75,000, and in 40.8% if it never came at all. A plan that bought the 10 payments in Treasuries first never missed one. Our timeline for that day doesn't dress it up: "first model of our original plan ... We changed strategy."

What we'd underestimated wasn't a crash so much as timing. With three-quarters in shares, every payment needed share values to be the right size on the right date, 10 times over, and one bad date was enough to miss. So we dropped the plan, before a single trade, and rebuilt it in a fixed order: the payments first, then the bottom of the range, then the top, then whatever Laura keeps.

The belief we'd leaned on turns out to have a name – the time-diversification fallacy. Paul Samuelson (1963) showed that someone who would refuse one favourable bet cannot rationally accept a long run of them. In other words, 10 years of growth was never going to make 10 dated payments safe by itself, however long it felt at the start.

The second lesson was more humbling. We had argued over whether the growth money should be 50%, 60% or 70% shares, and in our simulations that whole choice moved the median outcome by about $2,000 – while putting the payments first was worth the whole case. It taught us to weigh a decision by what it actually changes.
G4:
We'd love to say we got Laura's plan right the first time. We didn't, and the first version is worth showing.

On Sunday 27 September our plan put about three-quarters of the money in shares and trusted 10 years of growth to cover the 10 payments; we believed 10 years was long enough for shares to carry them. Before any trade, we tested it. In our simulations that day, it missed at least one payment in 3.2% of markets, in 13.7% if the 2028 deposit came in at $75,000, and in 40.8% if it never came. Buying the 10 payments in Treasuries first never missed one. Our timeline reads: "first model of our original plan ... We changed strategy." And we did, before a single trade.

Printing has the best picture we've found of what went wrong. In a knockout, the colour underneath leaves a hole for the black to fall into – and if the sheet slips even slightly, a thin white gap shows. Overprinting lays the black straight on top of the colour, so no gap can open. Our first plan was a knockout. Its danger wasn't a crash: with three-quarters in shares, each payment needed share values to be the right size on the right date, 10 times over, and a slip on any one date would show as a missed payment. The fix wasn't better shares. It was to print the payments over everything – inked first, in Treasuries she owns, where no slip can show – and only then the bottom of the range, the top, and what Laura keeps.

The belief underneath has a name, the time-diversification fallacy: Paul Samuelson (1963) showed that someone who would refuse one favourable bet cannot rationally accept a long run of them. And the question we'd argued over – 50%, 60% or 70% of the growth money in shares – moved the median by about $2,000 in our simulations, while printing the payments first was worth the whole case. That gap taught us to weigh a decision by what it changes.
K1:
Here's an argument we expect a judge to resist, because we resisted it ourselves: for Laura, more shares would be the risky choice.

The instinct is easy to understand. She has years before the building needs money, shares beat bonds over long stretches, and VT is sitting right there. So why does most of the 2028 deposit go into a Treasury fund that matures in late 2032 and earns, at best, what Treasuries earn?

Because of what that money is for. In 2031 Laura gives co-sponsors a figure she has to stand behind – and the only figures she can stand behind are ones she owns in Treasuries. So we ran the alternative. Take the roughly $111,700 left after the top-up and put three-quarters of it in shares, instead of about a quarter. At the median, she ends up with about $7,000 more in total – $198,000 against $191,000. Nice! But in a bad 1-in-20 future she has about $14,000 less, the range she can state shrinks from $95,000–$115,000 to $30,000–$85,000, and her contribution lands under $95,000 in about 62 futures out of 100, against about 3 under our plan. Go all the way to shares and the floor disappears altogether.

The shares, in other words, add to what Laura keeps, not to what she can promise. That doesn't make the opposite extreme free, either – putting all of it in the floor states a bigger single figure, $130,000, but leaves her with less overall in about 63 futures out of 100, and only around $9,000 of flexibility for overruns. Our split sits between the two, and we chose it knowing what each side costs.

So the risk we're steering around isn't really a crash – Laura's payments wouldn't notice one. It's standing in front of co-sponsors with a number the market later takes back.
K2:
Any illustrator will tell you that ink only goes one way. You can always add more; taking it off is another matter – as one put it, it 'is a lot more complicated (and messy)'. We think that's the most useful thing Laura's own trade can teach her about the 2031 range, and it settles an argument a judge might reasonably start: shouldn't someone with years to go hold more shares?

In our plan, ink means a figure she owns in Treasuries, paying on its date; pencil is anything still waiting on a market. Shares are pencil until half of them move into Treasuries before the 2031 meetings. So the question isn't really 'how much growth?' – it's 'how much can she ink?'

We tested it. Take the roughly $111,700 left after the top-up and put three-quarters in shares instead of about a quarter. At the median she ends up with about $7,000 more overall ($198,000 against $191,000) – but in a bad 1-in-20 future, $14,000 less. Worse, the range she can actually state drops from $95,000–$115,000 to $30,000–$85,000, and her contribution falls under $95,000 in about 62 futures out of 100, compared with about 3 under the plan. More pencil, less ink.

And because ink can't be taken back, the plan only ever adds it. Every end of the range is rounded down, anything above the top goes to her flexibility rather than to a co-sponsor, and half the shares stay in pencil on purpose – nobody is ever promised them. The other extreme isn't free: put it all in the floor and she inks a bigger single figure ($130,000), but ends up with less overall in about 63 futures out of 100 and only about $9,000 of flexibility.

So more shares wouldn't make Laura's promise bigger. Strangely enough, they'd make it smaller.
K3:
Our first plan was the obvious one. On 27 September we put about three-quarters of Laura's money into shares, reasoning that ten years was surely long enough for growth to carry ten payments of $50,000.

Then we tested it – before placing a single trade – and it failed its own test. In our simulations it missed at least one payment in 3.2% of markets. That sounds small, until you remember what's being missed: a payment Laura asked us to meet with a 'high degree of certainty'. And it got much worse the moment we stopped assuming her second deposit arrived in full – 13.7% if it came in at $75,000, and 40.8% if it never came at all. A plan that bought the ten payments in Treasuries first never missed one. Our timeline puts it bluntly: 'first model of our original plan ... We changed strategy.'

What surprised us most was what we'd been arguing about. We had spent real time on whether the growth money should be 50%, 60% or 70% shares – and that whole debate was worth about $2,000 at the median. Payments first was worth the entire case. Ever since, we've tried to ask what a decision actually changes before arguing about it.

Our instinct, it turns out, even has a name: the time-diversification fallacy. Paul Samuelson showed back in 1963 that if you'd refuse one favourable bet, you can't rationally accept a long run of the same bet – more years spread the risk over more dates, they don't make it disappear. We'd assumed time would do the work that only a matching Treasury can.

The order that came out of that Sunday has held since – payments first, then the bottom of Laura's range, then the top, then what she keeps – and every later choice in this report was built on top of it.
K4:
On 27 September our plan was about three-quarters shares, with ten years of growth expected to carry ten payments of $50,000. We tested it before a single trade, and it failed its own test: in our simulations it missed at least one payment in 3.2% of markets – 13.7% if the 2028 deposit came in at $75,000, and 40.8% if it never came. Buying the ten in Treasuries first never missed one. 'We changed strategy,' says our timeline, and we did, that day.

It took us a while to see why it failed, and Laura's trade explains it better than we can. In printing, a knockout leaves a hole in the colour for the black to drop into – and if the sheet slips even slightly, a thin white gap shows around the edge. Overprinting lays the black straight on top of the colour, so no gap can open at all. Our first plan was a knockout. On average the shares would have grown plenty. The danger was registration: each payment needed share values to be the right size on the right date, ten dates in a row, and a slip on any one of them would show. A crash wasn't really the problem – timing was.

So the fix wasn't better shares. It was to print the payments over everything: bought first, in Treasuries, where a slip in the market can't open a gap.

The other surprise was how little our own argument had mattered. We'd debated whether the growth money should be 50%, 60% or 70% shares, and that debate was worth about $2,000 at the median. Payments first was worth the whole case. Since then we've tried to ask what a decision changes before we argue about it – and the order that came out of that Sunday (payments, then the bottom of the range, then the top, then what she keeps) is the one every later page of this report sits on.
C1: We know Treasury bonds (including this one – maturing 2037) won't create wealth, but they will remove uncertainty, through duration-matching. In other words, we take Laura's requested 'high degree of certainty' to mean a near-ironclad guarantee, and we provide exactly that. Every year the bonds sit untouched is a good year – one less year of Laura's money being exposed to anything the restless markets might decide to do. Notably – Laura's payments are fixed in nominal dollars, so a nominal Treasury matches the liability perfectly, meaning we don't need TIPS, which would hedge against a nonexistent inflation risk.
C2: Some years, WInS lists no Treasuries maturing – so we purchased iShares iBonds (like IBTM for 2032) instead. Defined-maturity, investment-grade, liquid, cheap and transparent about yields, these behave a lot like bonds when held to their end – so we'll simply ignore price noise in the interim. Together, our T-Bonds and iBonds ensure each of Laura's payments rests on a dedicated instrument (not merely a forecast). The catch is, their terminal payout is a net asset value, as opposed to a promise of par – but in return we gain a level of liquidity which no odd-lot bond offers.
C3: VT is where we allow ourselves to be wrong – because it's the only investment not standing between Laura and a payment deadline. This ETF owns thousands of companies, diversified across countries and sectors, which means we can avoid paying the price for the vain illusion that we can pick winners, instead buying the entire market's growth premium at an expense ratio of just 0.06%, for a forecast return of about 7.5% a year (as per JPMorgan). The T-Bonds and iBonds already cover the operating commitments, so VT answers a different question – how generous can the facility contribution be?
X1: Pension funds cover fixed payments either by matching their bonds' average life to the payments and rebalancing as rates move, or by buying one bond per payment and holding it. We do the second, which needs no forecast or trading. In January 2027, her first $300,000 buys a ladder of Treasury bonds and Treasury funds with fixed end dates, each maturing just before a January payment. A Treasury held to maturity pays exactly what it promised, whatever markets do, so no payment depends on shares.
X2:
In 2031, Laura gives co-sponsors a range. The bottom is the floor, rounded down: money she already owns. The top adds half her shares, which move into Treasuries before she names it, because a number said aloud can't quietly be halved after a bad year. The other half stays hers and liquid, as a cushion if the building costs more in Taiwan dollars.

The ladder's one weakness is that it counts on reinvesting its bonds' interest; if rates fall and stay low, it can fall short. Before Laura names her range, we price that shortfall at the day's rates, add a margin, and move that much from her kept shares into Treasuries. Her spare money shrinks before her promise does, and if it can't cover the gap, the whole range comes down.
